title: Synapses & Neurotransmitters
summary: How one neuron talks to the next: release, receptors, and ending the signal.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Synapse

levels.kid:
Neurons do not actually touch each other. Between them is a teeny tiny gap. The meeting spot, gap and all, is called a **synapse**.

How does a message cross the gap? Most of the time, the first neuron squirts out tiny chemical messengers called **neurotransmitters**. They float across the gap and land on the next neuron, like a ball thrown across a stream and caught on the other side.

The neuron that throws is the **presynaptic** neuron ("pre" means before). The neuron that catches is the **postsynaptic** neuron ("post" means after).

A few special synapses are different. They have little tunnels that connect the two cells, so electricity can pass right through. Those are **electrical synapses**, and they are super fast.
levels.hs:
A **synapse** is the junction where a neuron passes a signal to another cell: another neuron, a muscle cell or a gland. The term was coined by Charles Sherrington in 1897. There are two kinds.

**Chemical synapses** (by far the most common in the human brain):
- The **presynaptic terminal** contains small sacs called **synaptic vesicles**, filled with neurotransmitter, plus many mitochondria for energy.
- The **synaptic cleft** is a gap of about 20–40 nanometers.
- The **postsynaptic membrane** has **receptors** that bind the neurotransmitter. In electron microscope images it looks thickened, called the postsynaptic density.

Chemical synapses are one-way, slightly slower (a delay of about 0.5–1 millisecond) and very flexible: they can amplify signals, invert them (excite or inhibit) and change strength with learning.

**Electrical synapses**:
- Two cells are linked by **gap junctions**, channels made of proteins called connexins, which let ions flow directly between cells.
- They are extremely fast, usually two-way, and good for synchronizing groups of cells, as in some brainstem nuclei, the retina and the heart muscle.

Synapses are also named by where they land: **axodendritic** (axon to dendrite, most common), **axosomatic** (axon to cell body) and **axoaxonic** (axon to another axon). The special synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fiber is the **neuromuscular junction**.
levels.college:
**Ultrastructure of a chemical synapse.**
- **Active zone**: a specialized patch of presynaptic membrane where vesicles dock and fuse. Scaffold proteins (RIM, Munc13, RIM-BP, ELKS, bassoon, piccolo) organize vesicles next to voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
- **Vesicle pools**: a readily releasable pool docked at the active zone, a recycling pool and a reserve pool tethered by synapsin to actin.
- **Cleft**: about 20 nm in CNS synapses, bridged by trans-synaptic adhesion molecules (neurexins–neuroligins, SynCAMs, LRRTMs) that align release sites with receptors.
- **Postsynaptic density (PSD)**: a protein-dense scaffold (PSD-95, Shank, Homer, SAP97) anchoring glutamate receptors, signaling enzymes such as CaMKII, and cytoskeleton.

**Gray's types.** Type I synapses (asymmetric, thick PSD, round vesicles) are usually excitatory and glutamatergic, mostly on dendritic spines. Type II synapses (symmetric, thin PSD, flattened or pleomorphic vesicles) are usually inhibitory and GABAergic, concentrated on the soma, proximal dendrites and AIS, where they powerfully control output.

**Electrical synapses.** Gap junctions consist of two hemichannels (connexons), each a hexamer of connexins; connexin-36 is the main neuronal connexin. They allow ions and small molecules to pass, are often bidirectional, have essentially no delay, and can be rectifying. They synchronize inhibitory interneuron networks, the inferior olive and retinal circuits.

**The neuromuscular junction (NMJ).** A model synapse: a single motor axon terminal releases acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors clustered on junctional folds of the motor end plate. Acetylcholinesterase in the basal lamina rapidly ends the signal. The NMJ has a high safety factor: each impulse releases far more transmitter than needed to reach threshold.

**Clinical windows.** Myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic AChR antibodies), Lambert–Eaton (presynaptic Ca2+ channel antibodies), botulism (blocks release) and mutations in neuroligins/neurexins linked to autism and schizophrenia illustrate how each synaptic component can fail.
levels.phd:
The synapse is a nanoscale machine whose geometry determines its computation.

**Nanocolumns.** Super-resolution imaging shows that release sites and postsynaptic receptor clusters are aligned in trans-synaptic "nanocolumns" roughly 80 nm wide, organized by RIM on the presynaptic side and PSD-95 on the postsynaptic side, linked by adhesion proteins. Because AMPA receptors have low glutamate affinity, a fusion event activates receptors effectively only within about 100 nm, so nanoscale alignment substantially controls synaptic strength. Misalignment may be a mechanism of synaptic weakening.

**Coupling distance.** The distance between Ca2+ channels and vesicle Ca2+ sensors (nanodomain vs microdomain coupling) sets release probability, speed and susceptibility to slow buffers like EGTA. Mature fast synapses tend toward tight nanodomain coupling.

**Diversity of synapses.** Synapses differ by orders of magnitude in release probability, number of release sites and short-term plasticity. The calyx of Held in the auditory brainstem, with hundreds of active zones, ensures faithful high-frequency transmission; cerebellar parallel fiber synapses have low release probability and facilitate. Mossy fiber boutons in the hippocampus are "conditional detonators."

**Electrical synapse plasticity.** Gap junction coupling is modulated by phosphorylation, dopamine and activity; mixed chemical–electrical synapses (Mauthner cell, mammalian brainstem) show that the old dichotomy is not absolute.

**Tripartite and quadripartite synapses.** Perisynaptic astrocyte processes and the extracellular matrix (perineuronal nets around parvalbumin interneurons) stabilize synapses and restrict plasticity. Digesting perineuronal nets with chondroitinase can reopen critical-period-like plasticity in adult visual cortex.

**Synaptopathies.** Many neurodevelopmental genes encode synaptic proteins: SHANK3 (Phelan–McDermid syndrome), NRXN1 deletions, NLGN3/4, SYNGAP1 (intellectual disability and epilepsy) and the enormous postsynaptic proteome implicated in schizophrenia genetics. Autoimmune encephalitides target synaptic proteins directly: anti-NMDA receptor, anti-AMPA receptor, anti-GABA-B and anti-GABA-A receptor encephalitis.

**Numbers.** The human cortex contains on the order of 10^14 synapses, and synaptic density peaks in childhood then is pruned through adolescence, especially in prefrontal cortex.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the synapse is where many neurological diseases, toxins and drugs act, and the location of failure produces distinct bedside patterns.

**Neuromuscular junction disorders** share fatigable weakness without sensory loss, but differ:
- **Myasthenia gravis** (postsynaptic, antibodies to AChR or MuSK): ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day, bulbar weakness, proximal weakness; reflexes normal. Repetitive nerve stimulation at low frequency shows a decrement; single-fiber EMG shows increased jitter. Look for thymoma with chest imaging.
- **Lambert–Eaton** (presynaptic): proximal leg weakness, reduced reflexes that transiently improve after brief exercise, dry mouth and other autonomic features. High-frequency stimulation or brief exercise produces an increment in CMAP amplitude. Search for small cell lung cancer.
- **Botulism** (presynaptic release failure): descending paralysis starting with cranial nerves (diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia), dilated unreactive pupils and constipation; infant botulism presents with constipation, poor feeding and weak cry. Treat with antitoxin and support breathing.

**Myasthenic crisis** is a neuromuscular emergency: watch forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force rather than oxygen saturation, which falls late. Several drug classes can worsen myasthenia, including aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium and some beta-blockers.

**Autoimmune synaptic encephalitis.** Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, often in young women and sometimes with an ovarian teratoma, evolves from psychiatric symptoms to seizures, dyskinesias (especially orofacial), autonomic instability and decreased consciousness. CSF and EEG help; the EEG may show "extreme delta brush." Early immunotherapy and tumor removal improve outcomes, so suspicion matters in any young patient with new psychosis plus neurological signs.

**Surgical relevance.** Neuromuscular blocking agents act at the NMJ; they eliminate EMG-based neuromonitoring and must be coordinated with the monitoring team. Patients with myasthenia are unusually sensitive to nondepolarizing blockers and resistant to succinylcholine.

**Pitfall:** pure ocular myasthenia can mimic a cranial nerve palsy; pupil involvement argues against myasthenia, because the pupil is spared in MG.

keyPoints: A synapse = presynaptic terminal, synaptic cleft and postsynaptic membrane
Chemical synapses use neurotransmitters, are one-way and plastic; electrical synapses use gap junctions and are fast
Gray type I (asymmetric) synapses are usually excitatory; type II (symmetric) usually inhibitory
The neuromuscular junction uses acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors
Myasthenia gravis, Lambert–Eaton and botulism are synaptic diseases of the NMJ

examples.src: Ptosis and diplopia that worsen by evening, normal pupils
examples.tr: Suggests myasthenia gravis, a postsynaptic NMJ disorder.
Electrical synapses that synchronize inhibitory networks.

lessons.title: Neurotransmitter Release

levels.kid:
How does a neuron throw its chemical messengers across the gap? Here are the steps.

1. The zap (action potential) arrives at the tip of the axon.
2. Special doors open and **calcium** rushes in. Calcium is the "go!" signal.
3. Tiny bubbles called **vesicles** are full of messengers. Calcium makes them bump into the edge of the cell and pop open.
4. The messengers spill out into the gap and float to the next neuron.

Afterward, the cell is very tidy. It pulls the bubble skin back in and refills it, like reusing a water balloon. That way it is ready to send the next message.

Some poisons, like the one that causes **botulism**, stop the bubbles from popping. Then no message gets through, and muscles cannot move.
levels.hs:
When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, it triggers neurotransmitter release through a precise sequence:

1. **Depolarization of the terminal** opens **voltage-gated calcium (Ca2+) channels**.
2. **Ca2+ enters** the terminal. Calcium is the key trigger; without extracellular Ca2+, release stops even if action potentials arrive.
3. **Vesicle fusion.** Synaptic vesicles docked at the **active zone** fuse with the membrane. Proteins called **SNAREs** act like zippers pulling the vesicle and cell membrane together, and a calcium sensor called **synaptotagmin** triggers the final fusion.
4. **Exocytosis.** Neurotransmitter spills into the synaptic cleft and diffuses to receptors on the postsynaptic cell. The whole process takes less than a millisecond.
5. **Recycling.** Vesicle membrane is retrieved by **endocytosis** (often with the protein clathrin), refilled with transmitter by transporters, and reused.

**Quantal release.** Neurotransmitter comes in packets: one vesicle = one **quantum**. Bernard Katz showed this at the frog neuromuscular junction, where tiny spontaneous "miniature" potentials each represent a single vesicle.

**Toxins:**
- **Botulinum toxin** and **tetanus toxin** cut SNARE proteins, blocking release. Botulinum blocks acetylcholine release at muscles (floppy paralysis). Tetanus toxin travels into the spinal cord and blocks release from inhibitory neurons (rigid spasms).
- **Black widow spider venom** (α-latrotoxin) causes massive release.

Medically, tiny injections of botulinum toxin (Botox) are used to treat muscle spasms, dystonia and chronic migraine.
levels.college:
**Calcium trigger.** Release depends steeply on Ca2+, roughly with the fourth power of Ca2+ concentration (Dodge and Rahamimoff), consistent with cooperative binding of several Ca2+ ions to the sensor. Presynaptic Cav2.1 (P/Q) and Cav2.2 (N) channels predominate at fast CNS synapses; local Ca2+ concentrations near open channels reach tens of micromolar within microseconds.

**Molecular machinery.**
- **SNAREs**: synaptobrevin (VAMP2) on the vesicle; syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 on the plasma membrane. They form a four-helix bundle that drives membrane fusion.
- **Munc18 and Munc13** chaperone and prime SNARE assembly; complexin clamps partially assembled SNAREs.
- **Synaptotagmin-1** binds Ca2+ through C2 domains and triggers synchronous release; synaptotagmin-7 and Doc2 contribute to asynchronous release.
- After fusion, **NSF** (an ATPase) and α-SNAP disassemble SNARE complexes for reuse.

**Toxins and their targets.** Botulinum toxins A and E cleave SNAP-25; B, D, F and G cleave synaptobrevin; C cleaves syntaxin (and SNAP-25). Tetanus toxin cleaves synaptobrevin but is transported retrogradely and transcytosed into inhibitory interneurons. α-Latrotoxin forces release through neurexin/latrophilin binding.

**Quantal analysis.** Mean quantal content m = n × p, where n is the number of release sites and p is release probability. Miniature end-plate potentials represent single quanta; evoked end-plate potentials are multiples of the quantal size q.

**Short-term plasticity.** Low-p synapses show **facilitation** with paired pulses (residual Ca2+ adds to the next spike's Ca2+); high-p synapses show **depression** (vesicle depletion). Post-tetanic potentiation follows high-frequency trains.

**Recycling routes.** Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (dynamin pinches off vesicles), ultrafast endocytosis within tens of milliseconds, bulk endocytosis during intense activity and possibly transient "kiss-and-run" fusion. Vesicles refill via vesicular transporters driven by a proton gradient from the V-ATPase: VGLUT (glutamate), VGAT (GABA/glycine), VAChT (ACh), VMAT2 (monoamines).

**Neuropeptides** are packaged in large dense-core vesicles, released farther from active zones and typically require higher-frequency firing.
levels.phd:
Neurotransmitter release is one of the best-understood molecular machines in biology, recognized by the 2013 Nobel Prize to Rothman, Schekman and Südhof, yet key questions remain open.

**Fusion mechanics.** How many SNARE complexes are needed per fusion event is debated (estimates range from one to around three for fast release, with more speeding fusion). Cryo-electron tomography shows docked vesicles held in a primed state by a ring-like arrangement of synaptotagmin and SNAREs under Munc13 control, poised to fuse within microseconds of Ca2+ entry. Whether synaptotagmin triggers fusion by bending membranes, releasing the complexin clamp, or both remains a live question.

**Release site models.** The "release site" is a structural and functional unit that can hold one docked vesicle at a time; refilling rates set sustained release. Release probability is heterogeneous even among boutons of the same axon, and is regulated by target identity (target-cell-specific plasticity).


**Presynaptic homeostatic plasticity.** At the Drosophila and mammalian NMJ, blocking postsynaptic receptors increases quantal content to restore evoked responses, via retrograde signals that increase presynaptic Ca2+ influx and readily releasable pool size. This compensation partly explains why early myasthenia can be clinically silent.

**Modulation.** Presynaptic GPCRs (GABA-B, mGluR2/3, CB1, A1 adenosine, α2-adrenergic, μ-opioid) inhibit release mainly through Gβγ inhibition of Cav2 channels and direct actions on SNAREs. Endocannabinoids released by depolarized postsynaptic neurons act retrogradely on CB1 to cause depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition or excitation.

**Disease.** Mutations in STXBP1 (Munc18-1), SNAP25, SYT1 and VAMP2 cause developmental epileptic encephalopathies, illustrating the dosage sensitivity of the release machinery. α-Synuclein, the protein aggregating in Parkinson's disease, normally binds vesicles and SNAREs and may chaperone SNARE assembly.
levels.expert:
Release biology translates directly into therapy and toxicology.

**Botulinum toxin as medicine.** Local injections produce a chemical denervation lasting roughly three months, until terminals sprout and the original endplate recovers. Indications include cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, hemifacial spasm, post-stroke spasticity, sialorrhea, chronic migraine and overactive bladder. Adverse effects reflect spread: dysphagia after neck injections, ptosis after forehead injections. Antibody formation can cause secondary non-response, which is why physicians avoid unnecessarily frequent boosters.

**Botulism.** Foodborne, wound (including injection drug use), infant and iatrogenic forms. Classic presentation: afebrile, symmetric descending paralysis beginning with cranial nerves, dilated poorly reactive pupils, dry mouth and constipation, with clear mentation. Electrodiagnosis shows small CMAPs with increment at high-frequency stimulation, like Lambert–Eaton. Treatment is early antitoxin (equine heptavalent for adults; human-derived botulism immune globulin for infants) plus ventilatory support; antitoxin stops progression but does not reverse existing paralysis.

**Tetanus.** Trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, painful spasms triggered by stimuli, and autonomic storms. Management: wound debridement, tetanus immune globulin, vaccination (infection does not confer immunity), antibiotics, benzodiazepines and often neuromuscular blockade with ventilation in a quiet ICU.

**Presynaptic drugs in neurology.** Levetiracetam and brivaracetam bind synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, reducing release during high-frequency firing; levetiracetam is widely used, including in neurocritical care, but behavioral side effects (irritability, mood change) are common. Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) blocks presynaptic K+ channels, prolonging depolarization and Ca2+ entry; it is used for Lambert–Eaton. Reserpine and tetrabenazine-class drugs (VMAT2 inhibitors such as deutetrabenazine and valbenazine) deplete monoamines and treat chorea and tardive dyskinesia, with depression as a key risk.

**Magnesium** competes with calcium at presynaptic channels; that is why high magnesium can worsen myasthenia and Lambert–Eaton and can cause weakness and areflexia when levels are high.

**Pitfall:** in suspected botulism, do not wait for confirmatory toxin assays before giving antitoxin.

keyPoints: An action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; Ca2+ entry triggers release
SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25) drive vesicle fusion; synaptotagmin is the Ca2+ sensor
Transmitter is released in quanta: one vesicle = one quantum
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNAREs to block ACh release (flaccid paralysis); tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory release (spastic paralysis)
Vesicles are recycled by endocytosis and refilled by vesicular transporters

Antiseizure drug that binds the vesicle protein SV2A.

lessons.title: Receptors & Postsynaptic Potentials

levels.kid:
When a messenger lands on the next neuron, it fits into a **receptor**, like a key into a lock.

Some locks are **fast doors**. The key turns and the door opens right away, letting ions rush in. Some locks are **slow doorbells**. The key rings a bell inside the cell, and helpers inside start a chain of jobs. That takes longer but can last longer too.

Some messages say "Go! Fire!" Those are **excitatory**. Some say "Stop! Calm down!" Those are **inhibitory**.

A neuron listens to thousands of go and stop messages at once. It adds them all up, like counting votes. If there are enough "go" votes to reach threshold, it fires. If not, it stays quiet.
levels.hs:
Neurotransmitters act by binding **receptors** on the postsynaptic membrane. There are two big families.

**1. Ionotropic receptors (ligand-gated ion channels)**
The receptor is itself an ion channel. When transmitter binds, the channel opens within about a millisecond. Fast and brief. Examples: nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, AMPA and NMDA glutamate receptors, GABA-A receptors.

**2. Metabotropic receptors (G-protein-coupled receptors, GPCRs)**
The receptor activates a G protein inside the cell, which triggers second messengers (like cAMP) or opens channels indirectly. Slower (tens of milliseconds to seconds) but longer-lasting and able to amplify signals. Examples: muscarinic ACh receptors, dopamine receptors, most serotonin receptors, GABA-B.

**Postsynaptic potentials:**
- **EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential)**: a small depolarization that pushes the neuron toward threshold, usually by letting Na+ in (e.g., glutamate on AMPA receptors).
- **IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential)**: a hyperpolarization or stabilization that pushes the neuron away from threshold, usually by letting Cl− in or K+ out (e.g., GABA on GABA-A receptors).

**Summation.** One EPSP is far too small to trigger an action potential. Neurons add inputs:
- **Temporal summation**: inputs arriving close together in time.
- **Spatial summation**: inputs arriving at the same time from different synapses.

The neuron integrates thousands of EPSPs and IPSPs at the axon initial segment. Whether a transmitter excites or inhibits depends on the receptor, not on the transmitter itself: acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle but slows the heart.
levels.college:
**Ionotropic receptor families.**
- **Cys-loop pentamers**: nicotinic AChR (muscle type α1₂β1δε in adults; neuronal α4β2, α7), GABA-A (commonly 2α, 2β, 1γ), glycine receptors, 5-HT3.
- **Ionotropic glutamate receptors (tetramers)**: AMPA (GluA1–4; most fast excitation; GluA2-lacking receptors are Ca2+-permeable), NMDA (GluN1 with GluN2A–D), kainate.
- **P2X** (ATP, trimers).

**NMDA receptors are coincidence detectors.** They need glutamate plus a co-agonist (glycine or D-serine) and depolarization to expel the Mg2+ block from the pore. They pass Ca2+ as well as Na+ and K+, linking activity to plasticity.

**Metabotropic receptors.** GPCRs couple to Gs (↑ adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, PKA; e.g., D1, β-adrenergic), Gi/o (↓ cAMP, opening GIRK K+ channels, closing Ca2+ channels; e.g., D2, GABA-B, μ-opioid, M2, α2) or Gq (phospholipase C → IP3 and DAG → Ca2+ release and PKC; e.g., M1, M3, α1, 5-HT2A, mGluR1/5).

**Reversal potential determines the sign.** A synaptic current drives Vm toward the receptor's reversal potential. AMPA/nicotinic channels (mixed cation, E_rev ≈ 0 mV) depolarize. GABA-A channels (Cl−, and some bicarbonate) have E_rev near −65 to −75 mV in mature neurons; if this is close to rest, opening them produces little voltage change but increases membrane conductance, **shunting inhibition** that cancels nearby EPSPs.

**Integration.** The membrane time constant (τ) sets the window for temporal summation; the length constant (λ) governs how much distal input decays before reaching the soma. Inhibitory synapses on the soma or AIS veto output more powerfully than distal ones.

**Receptor regulation.** Desensitization (receptors close despite bound agonist), internalization, phosphorylation and changes in subunit composition adjust synaptic strength. Receptor upregulation after chronic blockade, and downregulation after chronic stimulation, underlie tolerance and withdrawal phenomena seen with many CNS drugs.

**Examples of drug targets.** Benzodiazepines bind the α–γ2 interface of GABA-A receptors and increase opening frequency; barbiturates increase opening duration.
levels.phd:
Postsynaptic signalling is a problem of molecular kinetics, receptor diversity and dendritic geometry.

**Receptor kinetics shape synaptic computation.** AMPA receptor currents rise in about 0.2 ms and decay in a few ms; NMDA receptor currents rise slowly and decay over tens to hundreds of ms depending on GluN2 subunit (GluN2A faster than GluN2B). The slow NMDA component supports temporal integration, persistent activity models of working memory, and plasticity. Auxiliary proteins (TARPs such as stargazin, cornichons) modulate AMPA trafficking, gating and pharmacology.

**Receptor diffusion.** Single-particle tracking shows AMPA receptors diffuse laterally between synaptic and extrasynaptic sites; fast exchange of desensitized for naive receptors can contribute to recovery from paired-pulse depression. Synaptic strength therefore depends on receptor trapping by PSD scaffolds as much as on receptor number.

**Extrasynaptic and tonic signalling.** Extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors containing δ (with α4 or α6) or α5 subunits mediate tonic inhibition, sensitive to ambient GABA and to neurosteroids; this is a target of drugs such as ganaxolone and brexanolone/zuranolone for specific indications. Synaptic vs extrasynaptic NMDA receptor signalling has been proposed to promote survival vs death pathways respectively (the "location hypothesis"), though this is debated.

**Nonlinear dendritic integration.** Clustered synaptic input on thin dendrites can trigger local NMDA spikes, producing supralinear summation; dispersed input sums more linearly. Inhibition placed on the path between input and soma ("on-path" shunting) is especially effective. These nonlinearities make dendritic branches semi-independent computational subunits.

**Metabotropic signalling diversity.** GPCRs show biased agonism (preferential G protein vs β-arrestin signalling), heterodimerization (e.g., A2A–D2 in striatal indirect-pathway neurons, GABA-B obligate heterodimer of B1 and B2) and signalling from endosomes. Biased μ-opioid agonists were developed hoping to separate analgesia from respiratory depression; clinical results have been modest, challenging the original β-arrestin hypothesis.

**GABA excitatory under some conditions.** In development and in some pathological states (after injury, in some epileptic tissue), elevated intracellular Cl− shifts E_GABA positive, so GABA-A activation depolarizes, which may explain paradoxical responses to benzodiazepines in neonatal seizures.
levels.expert:
Receptor pharmacology is the vocabulary of neurological prescribing and the key to predicting adverse effects.

**GABA-A in practice.** Benzodiazepines are first-line for status epilepticus because they act within minutes. As seizures continue, synaptic GABA-A receptors are internalized while NMDA receptors are trafficked to the surface, so benzodiazepines lose efficacy the longer status lasts. Clinically: treat early and in adequate doses, then move promptly to a second-line agent; refractory status may require anesthetics is increasingly used for super-refractory cases. Chronic benzodiazepine use causes receptor adaptation; abrupt withdrawal can provoke seizures, as can alcohol withdrawal, whose treatment is also a GABA-A agonist.

**Nicotinic receptors.** Neuromuscular blockers are competitive (rocuronium, vecuronium) or depolarizing (succinylcholine). Succinylcholine can cause dangerous hyperkalemia in patients with upregulated extrajunctional receptors: denervation, burns, prolonged immobility, crush injury and some myopathies. Sugammadex reverses rocuronium and vecuronium by encapsulation; neostigmine reverses nondepolarizers by raising ACh.

**Muscarinic and dopamine receptors** explain many side effects. Anticholinergic burden (confusion, urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth, tachycardia) is a major cause of delirium in older adults. D2 antagonists (antipsychotics and antiemetics like metoclopramide) cause acute dystonia, akathisia, drug-induced parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia, and should be avoided in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia, where severe sensitivity reactions occur.

**NMDA receptors.** Memantine is used in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis shows what happens when these receptors are removed from synapses by antibodies.

**Serotonin receptors.** Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists for migraine, avoided in patients with coronary or cerebrovascular disease because of vasoconstriction. 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron) treat nausea; 5-HT2A antagonism is central to atypical antipsychotics.

**Pitfall:** flumazenil (benzodiazepine antagonist) can precipitate seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users or mixed overdoses, so it is not routine in undifferentiated coma.

keyPoints: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels (fast); metabotropic receptors are GPCRs (slow, amplifying)
EPSPs depolarize toward threshold; IPSPs hyperpolarize or shunt away from it
Neurons sum inputs temporally and spatially; the AIS decides whether to fire
NMDA receptors need glutamate, a co-agonist and depolarization to relieve the Mg2+ block
The receptor, not the transmitter, determines whether the effect is excitatory or inhibitory

lessons.title: Transmitter Classes & Signal Termination

levels.kid:
Your brain uses lots of different chemical messengers. Here are some stars:

- **Glutamate** is the main "go" messenger.
- **GABA** is the main "calm down" messenger.
- **Dopamine** helps with movement and with wanting things.
- **Serotonin** helps with mood and sleep.
- **Acetylcholine** tells muscles to move and helps with memory.

After a messenger does its job, it has to be cleared away, or the message would never stop. It is like erasing a whiteboard so you can write the next note. Sometimes the first neuron sucks the messenger back up to reuse it. Sometimes a helper chops it into pieces. Sometimes it just floats away. Some medicines work by slowing down this cleanup, so the messenger stays around longer.
levels.hs:
Neurotransmitters fall into a few major groups:

**1. Amino acids** (the workhorses of fast signaling):
- **Glutamate**: main excitatory transmitter in the brain.
- **GABA**: main inhibitory transmitter in the brain.
- **Glycine**: main inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem.

**2. Acetylcholine (ACh)**: muscle contraction at the neuromuscular junction, the parasympathetic nervous system, and attention and memory in the brain.

**3. Monoamines** (modulators that tune whole brain regions):
- **Dopamine**: movement, motivation and reward.
- **Norepinephrine**: alertness and the "fight or flight" response.
- **Serotonin (5-HT)**: mood, sleep, appetite.
- **Histamine**: wakefulness.

**4. Neuropeptides**: longer chains of amino acids, such as endorphins (natural pain relief) and substance P (pain signaling).

**5. Unusual messengers**: gases like **nitric oxide**, and lipids like **endocannabinoids**, which can travel backward across the synapse.

**Ending the signal** is as important as starting it:
- **Reuptake**: transporters pull the transmitter back into the presynaptic neuron or into glia. This is how most monoamines, glutamate and GABA are cleared.
- **Enzymatic breakdown**: acetylcholinesterase destroys ACh in milliseconds. Monoamine oxidase (MAO) and COMT break down monoamines.
- **Diffusion** away from the synapse.

Many drugs target these steps. SSRIs (like fluoxetine) block serotonin reuptake; cholinesterase inhibitors help in myasthenia gravis and Alzheimer's disease.
levels.college:
**Criteria.** A substance is accepted as a neurotransmitter when it is synthesized and stored presynaptically, released in a Ca2+-dependent way on stimulation, acts on specific postsynaptic receptors, and has a mechanism for removal; applying it mimics stimulation.

**Synthesis pathways (rate-limiting steps in bold).**
- Glutamate from glutamine (glutaminase) or the TCA cycle; GABA from glutamate by **glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD)**, which requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate).
- ACh from choline + acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase; **choline uptake (CHT1)** is rate-limiting.
- Catecholamines: tyrosine → L-DOPA (**tyrosine hydroxylase**) → dopamine (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase) → norepinephrine (dopamine β-hydroxylase, inside vesicles) → epinephrine (PNMT, mainly adrenal medulla).
- Serotonin: tryptophan → 5-hydroxytryptophan (**tryptophan hydroxylase**) → 5-HT (AADC).
- Histamine from histidine (histidine decarboxylase).

**Where the cell bodies are.** Dopamine: substantia nigra pars compacta and ventral tegmental area. Norepinephrine: locus coeruleus. Serotonin: raphe nuclei. ACh (CNS): nucleus basalis of Meynert and septal and brainstem nuclei. Histamine: tuberomammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus.

**Termination.**
- **Transporters (SLC6 family)**: DAT, NET, SERT for monoamines; GAT1–3 for GABA; GlyT1/2 for glycine. Glutamate is cleared by EAATs (SLC1 family), mostly EAAT2 on astrocytes.
- **Enzymes**: acetylcholinesterase (ACh → choline + acetate; choline is recycled); MAO-A (prefers serotonin and norepinephrine) and MAO-B (prefers dopamine) on mitochondria; COMT. Metabolites measured clinically: homovanillic acid (dopamine), vanillylmandelic acid and metanephrines (norepinephrine/epinephrine), 5-HIAA (serotonin).
- Neuropeptides are cleaved by extracellular peptidases and are not recycled; they are synthesized as prepropeptides in the soma and transported down the axon.

**Pharmacology at each step.** Synthesis (carbidopa blocks peripheral AADC so more L-DOPA reaches the brain), storage (VMAT2 inhibitors deplete monoamines), release (amphetamines reverse DAT/NET), reuptake (SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, cocaine), breakdown (MAO-B inhibitors such as selegiline and rasagiline, COMT inhibitors such as entacapone, cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil and pyridostigmine).
levels.phd:
Transmitter identity is less fixed, and signal termination more consequential, than the classic tables suggest.

**Co-release and co-transmission.** Many neurons release more than one transmitter. Midbrain dopamine neurons can co-release glutamate (via VGLUT2) and even GABA (via aldehyde dehydrogenase 1a1 synthesis and VMAT2 packaging, without VGAT); cholinergic interneurons co-release glutamate via VGLUT3. Peptides are commonly co-released with small-molecule transmitters at higher firing rates. Dale's principle (one neuron, the same transmitters at all its terminals) is broadly upheld in its modern form, but different transmitters can be sorted to distinct vesicles or terminals.

**Transmitter switching.** Activity and environmental changes can switch the transmitter a neuron uses (for example, hypothalamic neurons switching between dopamine and somatostatin with photoperiod in rodents), with matching postsynaptic receptor changes.

**Volume transmission.** Monoamines released from varicosities without classic synaptic specializations diffuse micrometers and act on extrasynaptic high-affinity receptors. Dopamine transporter density and spacing therefore define signal range; regional differences (high DAT in dorsal striatum, low in prefrontal cortex, where NET and COMT dominate dopamine clearance) explain why COMT genotype (Val158Met) affects prefrontal dopamine and cognition more than striatal dopamine.

**Transporters are dynamic.** DAT, NET and SERT are regulated by phosphorylation, trafficking and interacting proteins; amphetamines enter via the transporter, disrupt vesicular storage through VMAT2 and the vesicular pH gradient, and drive transporter-mediated efflux. Transporter structures (LeuT fold, SERT with bound SSRIs) clarified alternating-access mechanisms.

**Glutamate spillover and excitotoxicity.** Astrocytic EAAT2 clears most synaptic glutamate; its loss in ALS tissue and the efficacy (small) of riluzole hint at a role for excitotoxicity in motor neuron degeneration. During ischemia, transporters reverse and release glutamate.

**Unconventional messengers.** Nitric oxide is synthesized on demand by nNOS (coupled to NMDA receptors via PSD-95), diffuses through membranes and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase; endocannabinoids (2-AG, anandamide) are synthesized on demand from membrane lipids and act retrogradely on CB1; ATP and adenosine link activity to sleep pressure. These are not stored in vesicles, challenging classic criteria.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, transmitter systems explain symptoms, laboratory tests and some of the most dangerous drug interactions.

**Parkinson's disease therapy is applied transmitter biochemistry.** Levodopa is combined with carbidopa (a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor) so less dopamine forms outside the brain, reducing nausea and allowing more to cross the blood–brain barrier. COMT inhibitors (entacapone, opicapone) and MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide) prolong levodopa's effect and reduce "wearing off." High-protein meals can compete with levodopa for transport across gut and BBB amino acid carriers, a practical counseling point.

**Serotonin syndrome** results from excess serotonergic activity, typically when drugs combine: MAO inhibitors with SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, meperidine, linezolid (a weak MAO inhibitor) or methylene blue. Features: agitation, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrhea, tremor and especially lower-limb clonus and hyperreflexia, developing over hours. Distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (dopamine blockade, evolving over days, lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia). Stop the offending drugs; cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist) is used in moderate cases.

**Tyramine reaction.** Nonselective MAO inhibitors allow dietary tyramine (aged cheese, cured meats) to release norepinephrine, causing hypertensive crisis.

**Cholinergic and anticholinergic toxidromes.** Organophosphates and nerve agents irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase: miosis, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, salivation, urination, diarrhea, then fasciculations, weakness and paralysis. Treatment: atropine for muscarinic effects (titrated to drying of secretions) and pralidoxime to reactivate the enzyme before "aging" occurs, plus benzodiazepines for seizures. The anticholinergic toxidrome is the opposite: hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, urinary retention and delirium.

**Pyridoxine.** GAD needs vitamin B6; isoniazid toxicity depletes B6 and causes seizures refractory to standard drugs, treated with pyridoxine. Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy is a treatable cause of neonatal seizures.

**Tumor markers.** Catecholamine metabolites (metanephrines) detect pheochromocytoma; 5-HIAA detects carcinoid syndrome; urinary homovanillic acid and VMA support neuroblastoma diagnosis in children.

keyPoints: Glutamate is the main excitatory and GABA the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain; glycine is inhibitory in cord and brainstem
Monoamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, histamine) are modulators with small brainstem/midbrain source nuclei
Signals end by reuptake (transporters), enzymatic breakdown (AChE, MAO, COMT) or diffusion
Rate-limiting enzymes: tyrosine hydroxylase (catecholamines), tryptophan hydroxylase (serotonin), GAD (GABA, needs B6)
Many drugs act at synthesis, storage, release, reuptake or breakdown

test.q: The main excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain is:
test.explain: Glutamate drives most fast excitation.

test.q: The main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the SPINAL CORD is:
test.explain: Glycine (with GABA) dominates spinal and brainstem inhibition; GABA dominates in the brain.

test.q: Acetylcholine is cleared from the synapse mainly by:
test.explain: AChE splits ACh into choline and acetate within milliseconds; choline is recycled.

test.explain: NO is made on demand by NO synthase and is not stored in vesicles.

Block peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine
Increase MAO-B activity in the brain
Inhibit serotonin reuptake to ease mood

advancedTest.q: A patient on an MAO inhibitor is given linezolid and develops agitation, fever, diaphoresis and inducible lower-limb clonus within hours. Diagnosis?
advancedTest.explain: Rapid onset with clonus/hyperreflexia points to serotonin syndrome; linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor.

advancedTest.q: Why does the COMT Val158Met polymorphism affect prefrontal more than striatal dopamine signaling?
choices: The striatum has almost no dopamine for COMT to act on, so the variant has no effect
Prefrontal cortex has little DAT, so COMT contributes more to dopamine clearance there
COMT is expressed mainly in the striatum, so the variant changes striatal levels most
DAT is absent in the striatum, so striatal clearance relies on diffusion away
advancedTest.explain: Striatal clearance is dominated by DAT; prefrontal relies more on NET and COMT.

advancedTest.q: Seizures refractory to benzodiazepines after an isoniazid overdose are best treated with:
advancedTest.explain: Isoniazid depletes B6, impairing GAD and GABA synthesis.

advancedTest.q: In organophosphate poisoning, pralidoxime must be given early because:
choices: It only works before the phosphorylated enzyme 'ages'
It is active only when given orally
It blocks muscarinic receptors like atropine
It speeds up the 'aging' of inhibited AChE
advancedTest.explain: After aging, the AChE–phosphate bond cannot be broken by oximes.
